issues.legal_issue: A High Court may, on its own motion, withdraw a pending suit from a subordinate court and decide it itself.
material_facts: The suit was pending before a court subordinate to the High Court.
The High Court withdrew the suit to its own file and decided it on its own motion.
The appellant participated in the High Court proceedings without challenging its authority to withdraw the suit.
issues.conclusion: The High Court had jurisdiction under Section 24 of the Code of Civil Procedure to withdraw the pending suit on its own motion and dispose of it.
issues.legal_principle: Section 24(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure empowers the High Court, on its own motion and without notice, to withdraw a suit pending in a subordinate court and try or dispose of it. The decision in Khushro S. Gandhi v. N.A. Guzder was distinguishable because it did not concern an order under Section 24.

predicates.civil_suit_pending_in_subordinate_court: A civil suit was pending before a court subordinate to the High Court.
predicates.high_court_withdraws_suit_on_own_motion: The High Court withdrew the pending suit to itself on its own motion.

issues.definition: When a civil suit is pending in a subordinate court and the High Court withdraws it on its own motion, the High Court has jurisdiction to withdraw and decide the suit.

issues.legal_issue: A court may decide a suit on preliminary issues when admitted facts make those issues decisive of the suit.
material_facts: The parties did not dispute the earlier allotment-cancellation and mutation proceedings or their adjudication by revenue authorities.
The High Court had the suit record and admitted documents before it.
The issues of res judicata and maintainability could be determined on the admitted facts.
issues.conclusion: No particular procedure was required before the High Court disposed of the suit on the decisive preliminary issues.
issues.legal_principle: Order XIV Rule 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure permits a civil court to dispose of a suit on preliminary issues. Where facts are admitted, issues of res judicata, constructive res judicata, and maintainability can ordinarily be decided as preliminary issues. The High Court also referred to its inherent powers under Section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure.

rule.if: civil_suit_proceeding and suit_withdrawn_to_high_court and material_facts_admitted and threshold_issue_decisive

predicates.civil_suit_proceeding: The proceeding is a civil suit.
predicates.suit_withdrawn_to_high_court: The suit was withdrawn from a subordinate court to the High Court for decision.
predicates.material_facts_admitted: The parties admitted the material facts and the existence and adjudication of earlier proceedings.
predicates.threshold_issue_decisive: A preliminary issue concerning matters such as res judicata or maintainability could decide the suit.

issues.definition: When an admitted-fact civil suit withdrawn to the High Court presents a decisive threshold issue, the suit may be disposed of on preliminary issues.

issues.legal_issue: A party is barred from raising in a later civil suit a matter that could and ought to have been raised in earlier revenue proceedings within the revenue authorities’ jurisdiction, where those proceedings attained finality and their legality was not challenged.
material_facts: The revenue authorities conducted proceedings concerning cancellation of the appellant’s allotment and proceedings concerning mutation of the land.
The appellant could have challenged the respondent’s claimed relationship to the original allottee in those proceedings but did not do so.
The revenue authorities’ decisions were upheld, and the appellant’s review application was dismissed.
The later civil suit did not challenge the legality or validity of the earlier revenue proceedings.
issues.conclusion: The later challenge to the respondent’s relationship with the original allottee was barred by constructive res judicata.
issues.legal_principle: The principle of constructive res judicata bars matters that could and ought to have been raised in earlier proceedings before a competent authority. The revenue authorities had jurisdiction over the land-settlement and mutation proceedings and the jurisdictional question whether the land was subject to escheat, subject to review of the legality or validity of those proceedings in an appropriate civil suit. State of U.P. v. Amar Singh and Balwant Singh v. Daulat Singh were cited for the proposition that a mutation entry alone does not confer title; the Court distinguished that proposition from the effect of the final adjudications in this case.

rule.if: later_civil_suit_after_revenue_adjudication and revenue_authority_had_jurisdiction and party_could_raise_related_issue_earlier and earlier_decision_became_final and earlier_proceedings_not_challenged_in_later_suit

predicates.later_civil_suit_after_revenue_adjudicat: A party brought a civil suit after revenue authorities had adjudicated proceedings concerning the same land.
predicates.revenue_authority_had_jurisdiction: The revenue authorities had jurisdiction over the earlier land-settlement or mutation proceedings and the relevant jurisdictional question.
predicates.party_could_raise_related_issue_earlier: The party had an opportunity to raise the related issue in the earlier proceedings but did not do so.
predicates.earlier_decision_became_final: The earlier adjudication was not displaced and attained finality.
predicates.earlier_proceedings_not_challenged_in_la: The later civil suit did not challenge the legality or validity of the earlier proceedings.

issues.definition: If a party brings a later civil suit after a competent revenue adjudication, could have raised the related issue earlier, and leaves the final earlier decision unchallenged, the omitted issue is barred by constructive res judicata.

issues.legal_issue: A litigant may be prevented from pursuing repeated litigation that reopens a controversy already adjudicated and thereby abuses the court process.
material_facts: The appellant pursued successive proceedings concerning the same land after losing the allotment and mutation disputes.
The later suit sought relief concerning the same property and raised a related challenge that could have been raised earlier.
The earlier decisions had attained finality, but the appellant continued the litigation.
issues.conclusion: The later suit was an abuse of the court process, and the appellant could be prevented from pursuing that remedy.
issues.legal_principle: The Court distinguished abuse of process in the public interest from issue estoppel and estoppel by record, and held that a court may refuse a plaintiff the pursuit of a remedy to preserve finality in litigation. It relied on Johnson v. Gore Wood & Co.

rule.if: later_civil_suit_after_final_adjudication and same_controversy_reopened and related_claim_could_have_been_brought_earlier and repeated_litigation_continued

predicates.later_civil_suit_after_final_adjudicatio: A party brought a civil suit after an earlier adjudication of the controversy had become final.
predicates.same_controversy_reopened: The later suit sought to reopen a controversy concerning the same subject matter.
predicates.related_claim_could_have_been_brought_ea: The related claim could have been raised in the earlier proceedings.
predicates.repeated_litigation_continued: The party continued litigating the controversy through successive proceedings.

issues.definition: When a later civil suit reopens a final controversy through a related claim that could have been brought earlier, and the litigation has continued through successive proceedings, further litigation may be refused as an abuse.

issues.legal_issue: A person whose claim to an allotment has been rejected has no locus standi to challenge another claimant’s relationship with the original owner solely to contest that claimant’s entitlement to the land.
material_facts: The appellant’s allotment of part of the land was cancelled, and the cancellation was upheld through the revenue proceedings and before the High Court.
The appellant’s later suit sought a declaration that the respondent was not the original allottee’s daughter.
The appellant had no established entitlement to the land after the cancellation of his allotment.
issues.conclusion: The appellant lacked locus standi to challenge the respondent’s relationship with the original owner.
issues.legal_principle: The Court held that, after the appellant failed to establish his entitlement to the allotment, he had no locus standi to challenge the respondent’s relationship with the admitted owner as a means of contesting her entitlement. This conclusion followed from the final adjudication of the allotment dispute and the absence of any remaining established interest of the appellant in the land.

predicates.later_civil_suit_to_challenge_claimant_r: A party brought a later civil suit seeking to deny another claimant’s relationship with the original owner of the land.
predicates.claimant_entitlement_to_allotment_reject: The challenging party’s claim to an allotment of the land had been rejected in earlier proceedings.
predicates.challenger_has_no_established_interest_i: The challenging party had no established continuing interest in the land after the earlier rejection.

issues.definition: If a party brings a later civil suit to challenge another claimant’s relationship with the original owner after the party’s own allotment claim has been rejected and the party has no established interest in the land, the party lacks locus standi.

issues.legal_issue: A tenant who claims through a landlord cannot assert adverse possession against that landlord on the basis of the same title the tenant previously recognized.
material_facts: The appellant claimed to have been a tenant of the original allottee.
The appellant’s allotment had been made on the premise that the original allottee owned the land and died intestate without an heir.
The appellant later claimed to have acquired title by adverse possession.
issues.conclusion: The appellant, as a tenant who had claimed through the original allottee and relied on that allottee’s title for the allotment, could not sustain a claim of adverse possession against that title.
issues.legal_principle: The Court reasoned that a tenant could not question the landlord’s title and could not prevaricate from the position on which the tenant’s allotment had been made. The appellant’s own claim of adverse possession also necessarily acknowledged the original allottee’s title to the land.

predicates.adverse_possession_claim_proceeding: The proceeding includes a claim to have acquired title to land by adverse possession.
predicates.claimant_held_as_tenant_of_owner: The claimant held the land as a tenant of the person whose title is disputed.
predicates.claimant_relied_on_owner_title_for_land_: The claimant relied on the alleged owner’s title as the basis for a land claim or allotment.

issues.definition: When a claimant seeking adverse possession held as the owner’s tenant and relied on the owner’s title for a land claim, the claimant cannot assert adverse title against that owner.
